sweep_summary: One title-keyword item for Emberá-Chamí: Aguirre Licht (1992) 'Previsibilidad del acento en Emberá-Chamí', Lenguas Aborígenes de Colombia, Memorias 2: 31-62. Its existence and locus are confirmed twice (Fabre's Chocó bibliography; K10plus/IAI catalogue record of the host volume 'II Congreso del CCELA: Temas fonológicos..', Bogotá 1992, 227 pp., OCLC 248070934/253661242, held at Kiel and the Ibero-Amerikanisches Institut Berlin), but no digital copy exists anywhere reachable: no DOI (Crossref), not in HathiTrust (OCLC API), archive.org, LOC, Open Library or the Banco de la República library; Classified word-stress-of-this-language, print only, priority high (a 32-page paper on stress predictability by the language's main phonologist, predating both the 1995 phonology and the 2013 manual the catalog quotes). Side findings: (a) the IAI table-of-contents scan of the 1995 'Estudios fonológicos del grupo Choco' pins Aguirre Licht's stress rules to pp. 39-47 ('El acento', 'Reglas del acento en la palabra', 'Morfemas acentuados', 'Morfemas autoacentuados', 'El grupo acentual'), and HathiTrust holds that volume search-only (txu.059173001504988), so an interlibrary loan of pp. 31-62 of Memorias 2 and pp. 37-47 of Descripciones 8 would settle the 'weight-hedged' coding first-hand; (b) Páez Acevedo & Ibarra Zetter 2018 (Forma y Función, open access, downloaded) is a rhythm-class study, silent on stress placement. No first-hand stress statement was read in this search of works with stress in the title, so no new stress statement was found and the catalog's current deciding source (Aguirre Licht et al. 2013 manual, held held by the project with page scan) stands. Everything downloaded is under with listing file -> citation -> URL.

new_statements.quote: El acento es predecible gramaticalmente en verbos: /ko'si/ 'comió' /'kosima/ 'comió' /'kose/ 'coma' | /wa'si/ 'se fue' /'wasima/ 'se fue' /'wase/ 'váyase' | /widi'si/ 'pidió' /wi'disima/ 'pidió' /'wi'dise/ 'pida' [...] El acento es variable en palabras que no son verbos, cuando son expresadas tanto en aislamiento como en la mayoría de las frases controladas. [...] En muchas palabras de dos o tres sílabas (que no son verbos) no se nota ningún acento cuando son expresadas en aislamiento. En palabras de cuatro o cinco sílabas casi siempre se da un acento aunque no ocurre en una sílaba fija. [...] En casos en que se da el acento, el núcleo de la sílaba acentuada es más largo en duración y más fuerte que las sílabas inacentuadas.
new_statements.translation: Stress is grammatically predictable in verbs: /ko'si/ 'ate' /'kosima/ 'ate' /'kose/ 'eat!' | /wa'si/ 'went' /'wasima/ 'went' /'wase/ 'go!' | /widi'si/ 'asked' /wi'disima/ 'asked' /'wi'dise/ 'ask!' [...] Stress is variable in words that are not verbs, when uttered both in isolation and in most controlled phrases. [...] In many two- or three-syllable words (that are not verbs) no stress is noticed when they are uttered in isolation. In words of four or five syllables a stress almost always occurs, though not on a fixed syllable. [...] Where stress occurs, the nucleus of the stressed syllable is longer in duration and stronger than the unstressed syllables.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so nothing to contradict. Gralow 1976 supplies the first primary statement: stress is grammatically conditioned in verbs and variable/non-fixed in non-verbs, with weak or absent word stress on short non-verbs. Note the IAI table of contents already held by the project shows Aguirre Licht 1995 ('Fonología del ëbëra-chami de Cristianía', with sections on accented/unaccented/self-accented morphemes and 'funciones del acento') and Aguirre Licht 1992 'Previsibilidad del acento en Emberá-Chamí' treat stress as morphologically determined too, but those texts were not opened.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed word-stress position. In verbs the stress position is determined by the grammatical form (the suffix pattern): the finite past form in -si takes final stress (ko'si, wa'si, widi'si), the -ima past form and the imperative in -e take stress on the root (a stem-initial or stem syllable: 'kosima, 'wasima, 'kose, 'wase; wi'disima, 'wi'dise). In non-verbs stress is variable: 2-3 syllable words often show no audible stress in isolation, 4-5 syllable words almost always carry one stress but on no fixed syllable; the author marks it where it appears most often. Phonetic correlates: longer, stronger stressed nucleus; high pitch when word stress coincides with the phrase accent. Phrase level (p. 40): the phrase nucleus may be any of the last four syllables of the phrase and carries lengthening, intensity and high tone; intonation contours (Pike numbers) are described on pp. 41-42.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned at word level. Phrase accent ('acento principal de la frase') is described as stronger than word stress and can fall on any of the four final syllables of the phrase (p. 40).
new_statements.exceptions: Author flags the verb data as provisional ('Es posible que los ejemplos de la primera columna funcionan en un nivel gramatical distinto.. Se espera un análisis más a fondo'), and says further research may reveal more about non-verb stress. Many 2-3 syllable non-verbs show no stress in isolation.
new_statements.identity_note: Gralow 1976 describes Chamí as spoken in the Municipio de Pueblo Rico, Risaralda (Humaca and Curembará river areas, fieldwork June-Nov 1973) and San Antonio del Chamí, Risaralda (April-July 1974); consultants María Celina Bigamá, Juan José Tamaniza, Juana María Tamaniza (p. 30). This is Chamí proper (Risaralda), the same variety as Glottolog embe1262, not the Cristianía (Antioquia) community that Aguirre Licht 1995 and Herrera 2002 describe.

tone_statements.citation: Constenla Umaña, Adolfo & Margery Peña, Enrique. 1991. Elementos de fonología comparada chocó. Revista de Filología y Lingüística de la Universidad de Costa Rica 17(1-2): 137-191.
tone_statements.quote: En general, el tono parece ser más importante que la intensidad (véase, por ejemplo, Rex y Schöttelndreyer 1973: 79) en la manifestación fonética del acento y ciertas observaciones de Loewen (1958: 20, nota 4) sugieren incluso la posibilidad de que el sambú sea una lengua tonal [...]. No obstante, por el momento, todos los autores coinciden en asignar a las lenguas la condición de acentuales [...]. En dichas palabras, en los conjuntos de cognados, el acento recae en la penúltima sílaba casi sin excepciones en saija y chamí (en esta lengua en los datos de Pardo y de Gralow, pero no en los de Caudmont), en tanto que en catío y sambú puede recaer lo mismo en la penúltima que en la última.
tone_statements.translation: In general, pitch seems to be more important than intensity (see e.g. Rex & Schöttelndreyer 1973: 79) in the phonetic manifestation of the accent, and certain observations of Loewen (1958: 20, n. 4) even suggest the possibility that Sambú is a tone language [...]. Nevertheless, for the moment, all authors agree in assigning the languages the status of accentual (stress) languages [...]. In such words, in the cognate sets, the accent falls on the penultimate syllable almost without exception in Saija and Chamí (in this language in Pardo's and Gralow's data, but not in Caudmont's), whereas in Catío and Sambú it may fall on either the penult or the final syllable.
